sections.applicability: Applies when estimating undrained shear strength of cohesive soils using SPT N values, particularly for overconsolidated clays where PI data are also available.

sections.title: Correlations with Dilatometer
sections.summary: Summarizes empirical correlations for estimating undrained shear strength of overconsolidated clays from dilatometer horizontal stress index (KD) and dilatometer modulus (ED). Table 8-11 presents three source correlations: Marchetti (1980) and Kamei and Iwasaki (1995) using KD-based su/σ′v expressions, and Iwasaki and Kamei (1994) using ED directly for su in kPa.
sections.body: The undrained shear strength of overconsolidated clays has been correlated to the horizontal stress index (KD) and the dilatometer modulus (ED) as summarized in Table 8-11.
key_points: Marchetti (1980): (su/σ′v)OC = 0.22·(0.5·KD)^1.25 ≈ (su/σ′v)NC·(0.5·KD)^1.25, using KD from dilatometer.
Kamei and Iwasaki (1995): (su/σ′v)OC = (0.35·KD − 0.47)^1.14, an alternative KD-based power law.
Iwasaki and Kamei (1994): su = 0.018·ED (kPa), a direct correlation using dilatometer modulus.
All three correlations target overconsolidated clays; KD and ED must be derived from dilatometer testing.
tables: Table 8-11 Undrained Shear Strength Correlations to Dilatometer
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating undrained shear strength of overconsolidated clays from dilatometer test results (KD or ED).

sections.title: Consolidation Parameters
sections.summary: Parent section covering all consolidation parameters needed for settlement analysis, including compression/recompression indices for fine- and coarse-grained soils, constrained modulus correlations from SPT and CPT, and the coefficient of secondary compression. Provides typical values, index-property correlations, and in-situ test correlations for practical geotechnical design.
key_points: Covers Cc, Cr, Cεc, Cεr, constrained modulus (Mds), and secondary compression coefficient (Cα/Cεα) for a full range of soil types.
Provides both typical tabulated values and empirical correlations with index properties and in-situ tests.
Applicable to fine-grained (clays/silts) and coarse-grained (sands) soils across normally consolidated and overconsolidated ranges.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever consolidation parameters must be estimated for settlement calculations in fine- or coarse-grained soils.

sections.title: Compression and Recompression Indices – Fine-Grained
sections.summary: Defines the compression index (Cc) and recompression index (Cr) as slopes of the e vs. log(σʹv) plot for fine-grained soils, and introduces the modified indices Cεc and Cεr (compression/recompression ratios) normalized by (1+e0). These parameters govern settlement calculations in both normally consolidated and overconsolidated clay ranges.
sections.body: The compression index (Cc) is the slope of the virgin consolidation line of the e vs. log(σʹv) plot. The recompression index (Cr) is the slope of the recompression line of the e vs. log(σʹv) plot. These parameters are used to calculate the compression of the clay when subjected to an increase in stress in the normally consolidated and overconsolidated ranges (See Section 5-5.2.1). An alternative of the compression and recompression indices are the modified compression index (Cεc) and modified recompression index, Cεr (a.k.a., compression and recompression ratio). The modified compression and recompression indices are equal to the compression and recompression indices divided by (1+e0), respectively. These are the slopes of the compression and recompression curves when vertical strain is used instead of void ratio.
key_points: Cc = slope of the virgin consolidation line on the e vs. log(σʹv) plot; Cr = slope of the recompression line.
Modified indices Cεc = Cc/(1+e0) and Cεr = Cr/(1+e0) use vertical strain instead of void ratio.
Used with Section 5-5.2.1 methods to compute settlement in NC and OC clay.
sections.applicability: Applies to fine-grained soils (clays and silts) when calculating primary consolidation settlement.

sections.title: Typical Values
sections.summary: Provides a tabulated summary of typical Cc values for a wide range of undisturbed clays and silts, including Boston Blue Clay, Chicago clay, Mexico City Clay, organic soils, peat, and sands. Values span from 0.02 for dense uniform sand to over 10 for peat, illustrating the wide variability in compressibility across soil types.
sections.body: Typical values of the compression index for different clays and silts are summarized in Table 8-12.
key_points: Cc for normally consolidated medium-sensitive clays typically ranges from 0.2 to 0.5.
Organic clays (OH) have Cc > 4.0; peat (Pt) ranges from 10 to 15.
Dense uniform sands (SP) have very low Cc of 0.02–0.03, reflecting much lower compressibility than fine-grained soils.
Na-Montmorillonite has an exceptionally high Cc of 2.6 among mineral clays.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting a preliminary or reference Cc value for a specific clay or silt type without laboratory test data.

sections.title: Correlations with Index Properties
sections.summary: Summarizes numerous empirical correlations for estimating Cc and Cr from index properties (liquid limit, initial void ratio, natural water content, plasticity index, specific gravity, clay fraction, and combinations thereof). Highlights variability among correlations, notes that water-content-based Cc correlations show better agreement, and introduces Burland's (1990) intrinsic compression line (ICL) and sedimentation compression line (SCL) framework using Equations 8-27 through 8-30.
sections.body:
Many relationships have been developed to estimate the compression and recompression indices based on parameters, such as water content, liquid limit, and void ratio. Some of these correlations are summarized in Table 8-13 and Table 8-14 and plotted in Figure 8-33 thru Figure 8-38. As can be seen from these plots, the presented correlations estimate values of compression and recompression indices that vary significantly. For the compression index, the correlations using the natural water content tend to be in closer agreement compared to those based on other index properties. Prior to use, the soil type(s) used to develop the correlations and the sensitivity of the project to errors in the prediction of settlement should be considered to determine if the intended application matches.

Leroueil et al. (1983) showed that the sensitivity of the clay also affects the value of the compression index, especially for marine deposits. The results presented in Figure 8-39 show a significant effect of the sensitivity on the compression index.

Lambe and Whitman (1969) presented typical ranges of the modified compression index of clays as a function of the natural water content and these are shown in Figure 8-40.

Burland (1990) compiled data from normally consolidated clays, both undisturbed and reconstituted at a liquidity index ranging from 1 to 1.5. Recognizing that vertical stresses between 100 and 1000 kPa control most consolidation calculations, he defined the normally consolidated void ratios at these stresses as e*100 and e*1000, respectively. From these void ratios, the intrinsic compression index was defined as Eq. 8-27. By normalizing the current void ratio with respect to e*100, Burland defined the void index as Eq. 8-28. With the data normalized in this way, he defined the sedimentation compression line (SCL) and intrinsic compression line (ICL), which describe the typical variation of the in situ void index (Iv0) with effective stress for a wide range of clays. The SCL represents the typical relationship for the compression of naturally sedimented clays. The ICL represents the typical relationship for the compression of remolded clays. Burland's SCL and ICL are plotted in Figure 8-41.

While the values of e*100 and C*c are best determined from laboratory tests, Burland (1990) found that these parameters could be estimated from the void ratio at the liquid limit (eL) by Eq. 8-29 and Eq. 8-30.

Using Equations 8-28 through 8-30 and the relationships shown in Figure 8-41, the virgin consolidation line can be approximated solely based on liquid limit for both freshly deposited soils (using ICL) or structured, aged deposits (using SCL). This approach is particularly useful for validation of laboratory consolidation tests. Examples of the ICL and SCL for liquid limits ranging from 25 to 125 are plotted in Figure 8-42.
key_points: Natural water content-based correlations for Cc show better mutual agreement than liquid limit or void ratio-based correlations.
Clay sensitivity significantly affects Cc, especially for marine deposits (Leroueil et al. 1983).
Burland's (1990) void index framework normalizes compression behavior across clay types using e*100 and C*c, estimated from eL (Eqs. 8-27 to 8-30).
ICL describes remolded clay compression; SCL describes naturally sedimented clay compression — both approximable from liquid limit alone.
Approach useful for validating laboratory consolidation test results.

equations.description: Intrinsic compression index defined as C*c = e*100 − e*1000, where e*100 and e*1000 are intrinsic void ratios at 100 kPa and 1000 kPa, respectively.
Void index Iv = (e − e*100) / C*c, normalizing current void ratio with respect to the intrinsic void ratio at 100 kPa and the intrinsic compression index.
Intrinsic void ratio at 100 kPa estimated from void ratio at liquid limit: e*100 = 0.109 + 0.679eL − 0.089eL² + 0.016eL³.
Intrinsic compression index estimated from void ratio at liquid limit: C*c = 0.256eL − 0.04.

sections.applicability: Applies when laboratory consolidation test data are unavailable and Cc or Cr must be estimated from routine index properties for fine-grained soils.

sections.title: Compression and Recompression Indices – Coarse-Grained
sections.summary: Notes that coarse-grained soil compressibility is significantly lower than fine-grained soils and is normally not characterized by Cc and Cr. Recommends modulus-based methods (Chapter 5) instead. Provides tabulated modified compression index (Cεc) values for saturated NC sands as a function of soil gradation and relative density, and compressibility data (e0, Cc, Cr) for six specific sands.
sections.body: The compressibility of coarse-grained soils is normally significantly smaller than that from fine-grained soils. The compressibility of coarse-grained soils is not typically defined in terms of the compression and recompression indices. Instead the modulus-based methods presented in Chapter 5 are employed. The constrained modulus for coarse-grained soils is usually stress dependent (Kulhawy and Mayne 1990) and may be estimated using correlations in the following section. If required, typical values for the modified compression index of coarse-grained soils are summarized in Table 8-15 and Table 8-16.
key_points: Coarse-grained soil compressibility is much smaller than fine-grained soils and is not routinely expressed as Cc or Cr.
Modulus-based methods from Chapter 5 are preferred for sands and gravels.
Modified compression index Cεc for NC sands decreases significantly with increasing relative density (Dr).
Table 8-15 provides Cεc by gradation and Dr; Table 8-16 provides Cc and Cr for six specific research sands.
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating compressibility parameters for coarse-grained soils (sands and gravels) in settlement calculations.

sections.title: Constrained Modulus
sections.summary: Defines the secant drained constrained modulus (Mds) per Janbu (1963) as a function of vertical effective stress and modulus number (m), providing both linear and nonlinear forms. Relates modulus number to void ratio, porosity, and natural water content through figures. Serves as the parent section for SPT- and CPT-based correlations for Mds.
sections.body:
The secant drained constrained modulus (Mds) was found to be a function of the vertical effective stress (σʹv) and a modulus number (m) by Janbu (1963). The constrained modulus for normally consolidated clays, silts, and sands is related in either a linear or nonlinear fashion to vertical effective stress by Eq. 8-31 or Eq. 8-32.

Janbu (1963) related the modulus number to the void ratio (or porosity) and the natural water content as shown in Figure 8-43 and Figure 8-44, respectively. In addition, Janbu (1985) presented the relationship for the modulus number of NC silts and sands as a function of the porosity, as presented in Figure 8-45.
key_points: Mds = m·σʹv (linear, Eq. 8-31) or Mds = m·Pa·(σʹv/Pa)^0.5 (nonlinear, Eq. 8-32) depending on soil type.
Modulus number m is correlated to void ratio, porosity, and natural water content for NC soils via Janbu's figures.
Constrained modulus for coarse-grained soils is stress dependent and typically estimated from in-situ tests.

equations.description: Linear constrained modulus: Mds = m · σʹv, where m is the modulus number and σʹv is vertical effective stress.
Nonlinear constrained modulus: Mds = m · Pa · (σʹv / Pa)^0.5, where Pa is atmospheric pressure, accounting for stress-dependent stiffness.

sections.applicability: Applies to NC clays, silts, and sands when estimating constrained modulus for settlement analysis using Janbu's modulus number approach.

sections.title: Correlations with Standard Penetration Test
sections.summary: Presents Stroud's (1974) correlation of the constrained modulus of clays to SPT N-value and an empirical coefficient f dependent on plasticity index (PI). Notes that Kulhawy and Mayne (1990) found Stroud's correlation unreliable and recommend using it with caution.
sections.body: Based on results from nine British clays, Stroud (1974) correlated the constrained modulus of clays to the SPT N value as Eq. 8-33, where f is an empirical coefficient related to plasticity index from Figure 8-46, Pa is atmospheric pressure, and N is SPT blow count. According to Kulhawy and Mayne (1990), Stroud's correlation is not very reliable and should be used with caution.
key_points: Mds = f · N · Pa, where f is read from Figure 8-46 as a function of plasticity index.
Developed from nine British clays; reliability is limited — use with caution (Kulhawy and Mayne 1990).
f decreases with increasing PI, reflecting reduced stiffness in more plastic clays.

equations.description: SPT-based constrained modulus for clays: Mds = f · N · Pa, where f is an empirical PI-dependent coefficient (Figure 8-46) and Pa is atmospheric pressure.

sections.applicability: Applies when estimating constrained modulus of clays from SPT N-values and plasticity index in the absence of laboratory or CPT data.

sections.title: Correlations with Cone Penetration Test
sections.summary: Presents CPT-based correlations for constrained modulus using the general form Mds = α · qc, where α is an empirical coefficient ranging from 0.4 to 8 depending on soil type. Discusses Kulhawy and Mayne (1990) normalized correlation for clays using pore-pressure-corrected tip resistance (qt) from CPTu. Provides Figure 8-47 for graphical determination.
sections.body:
Numerous correlations have been presented to estimate the value of constrained modulus using the results from the cone penetration tests. Most of these correlations use the form of the equation shown below (Eq. 8-34), where Mds is the constrained modulus, qc is the cone tip resistance, and α is an empirical coefficient.

Mitchell and Gardner (1975) compiled values of α for different soils and showed that α can range from 0.4 to 8. In most cases, α is between 1 and 3. These values were obtained using a variety of cones with different geometries and testing procedures.

Kulhawy and Mayne (1990) presented the correlation shown in Figure 8-47 to obtain the constrained modulus of clays based on CPTu data in the form of tip resistance corrected for pore pressure and overburden stress.
key_points: General form: Mds = α · qc, with α ranging 0.4 to 8; most soils fall between α = 1 and 3.
α values compiled by Mitchell and Gardner (1975) vary with soil type and cone geometry — check applicability before use.
Kulhawy and Mayne (1990) provide a normalized CPTu-based chart correlation for clays using corrected tip resistance qt (Figure 8-47).

equations.description: CPT-based constrained modulus: Mds = α · qc, where qc is cone tip resistance and α is an empirical soil-dependent coefficient.

sections.applicability: Applies when estimating constrained modulus from CPT or CPTu data for clays and other soils.

sections.title: Coefficient of Secondary Compression
sections.summary: Defines the coefficient of secondary compression (Cα or Cεα) for estimating post-primary-consolidation creep settlement. Presents Mesri's (1973) correlation linking Cεα to natural water content (Eq. 8-35), the roughly constant ratio Cα/Cc for a given soil (Mesri and Godlewski 1977), and Table 8-17 tabulating Cα/Cc for natural clays, silts, organic soils, and peats.
sections.body:
The coefficient of secondary compression defines the settlement as a function of time after primary consolidation is completed. As with the compression ratios, the coefficient of secondary compression can be defined as a function of strain (Cεα) or as a function of the void ratio (Cα). See Section 5-5.4 for more details.

Mesri (1973) summarized the data shown in Figure 8-48 to estimate the coefficient of secondary compression of NC clays using the natural water content. Based on that data, the modified coefficient of secondary compression can be estimated as Eq. 8-35.

According to Kulhawy and Mayne (1990), Cεα ranges from 0.0005 and 0.001 for most overconsolidated clays. The ratio of the coefficient of secondary compression to the compression index (Cα / Cc = Cεα / Cεc) is more or less constant for a given soil (Mesri and Godlewski 1977). Values of Cα / Cc are summarized in Table 8-17. Another correlation for the coefficient of correlation for silts and clays is presented in Figure 8-49.
key_points: Cεα = 0.0001 · wn (Eq. 8-35) estimates modified secondary compression coefficient from natural water content for NC clays.
For most OC clays, Cεα ranges from 0.0005 to 0.001 (Kulhawy and Mayne 1990).
The ratio Cα/Cc (= Cεα/Cεc) is approximately constant for a given soil — enables estimation of Cα from measured Cc.
Inorganic clays: Cα/Cc ≈ 0.025–0.075; peats: Cα/Cc ≈ 0.035–0.10 (Table 8-17).
Figure 8-49 provides an additional graphical correlation for Cα in silts and clays.

equations.description: Modified secondary compression coefficient for NC clays: Cεα = 0.0001 · wn, where wn is natural water content (in %).

sections.applicability: Applies when estimating secondary (creep) compression settlement after primary consolidation is complete, particularly for NC clays, organic soils, and peats.

sections.title: Elastic Parameters
sections.summary: Container section covering elastic parameters for soil: Young's modulus (E), bulk modulus (K), shear modulus (G), and Poisson's ratio (ν). Presents correlations and typical values for fine-grained (undrained) and coarse-grained (drained) soils, drawing from field tests, lab tests, and load tests.
key_points: Four elastic parameters are addressed: Young's modulus (E), bulk modulus (K), shear modulus (G), and Poisson's ratio (ν).
Relationships between all four parameters are tabulated in Table 8-18.
Subsections address undrained modulus for fine-grained soils and drained modulus for coarse-grained soils.
Correlations are presented from SPT, pressuremeter, and load tests.
sections.applicability: Applies when elastic parameters are needed for any soil type in geotechnical analysis.

sections.title: Definitions
sections.summary: Defines the four common elastic parameters used in soil mechanics — Young's modulus (E), bulk modulus (K), shear modulus (G), and Poisson's ratio (ν) — and presents their interrelationships in Table 8-18. Explains the distinction between undrained and drained Young's modulus for fine-grained soils and notes that shear modulus is drainage-independent.
sections.body:
Correlations to four elastic parameters will be presented in this section: (1) Young's modulus (E) is the ratio of the change in normal stress in a given direction to the strain in the same direction within the elastic range; (2) bulk modulus (K) is the change in mean stress divided by the corresponding volumetric strain; (3) shear modulus (G) is the ratio of the change shear stress divided by the shear strain caused by that stress; and (4) Poisson's ratio (ν) is the ratio of the lateral strain to the axial strain caused by a change of stress. The relationships between these parameters are summarized in Table 8-18.

In fine-grained soils, the value of the Young's modulus from field testing is normally derived under undrained conditions (Eu). Assuming a Poisson's ratio for undrained conditions of 0.5, the Young's modulus under drained conditions can be found using Eq. 8-36.

The shear modulus represents the response of the soil skeleton and it is independent of drainage conditions (i.e., G = Gu) (Kulhawy and Mayne 1990). Assuming a Poisson's ratio for undrained conditions of 0.5, the relationships in Table 8-18 indicate that Eu is three times greater than the shear modulus. According to Kulhawy and Mayne (1990), the undrained Young's modulus of soils is stress path dependent.
key_points: Young's modulus (E): ratio of normal stress change to strain in same direction within elastic range.
Bulk modulus (K): change in mean stress divided by volumetric strain.
Shear modulus (G): ratio of shear stress change to resulting shear strain; drainage-independent (G = Gu).
Poisson's ratio (ν): ratio of lateral strain to axial strain under applied stress.
For fine-grained soils, drained E is derived from undrained Eu using Eq. 8-36 with assumed undrained ν = 0.5.
Eu = 3G when undrained ν = 0.5; undrained Young's modulus is stress path dependent (Kulhawy and Mayne 1990).

equations.description: Converts undrained Young's modulus (Eu) to drained Young's modulus (E) using drained Poisson's ratio (ν), assuming undrained ν = 0.5: E = Eu / (2(1+ν)/3)

sections.applicability: Applies when converting between elastic parameters or between undrained and drained Young's modulus for fine-grained soils.

sections.title: Undrained Young's Modulus of Fine-Grained Soils
sections.summary: Container section presenting methods to estimate the undrained Young's modulus (Eu) of fine-grained soils, including typical values, correlations with undrained shear strength, correlations with SPT and pressuremeter tests, and back-calculation from load tests on deep and spread foundations.
key_points: Eu for fine-grained soils is addressed through typical values, shear strength correlations, in-situ test correlations, and load test back-calculations.
Multiple sources (USACE, Kulhawy and Mayne, Duncan and Buchignani, Ohya et al., Poulos and Davis, Callanan and Kulhawy) are referenced.
Subsections cover typical values, shear strength correlations, SPT/PMT correlations, and load test correlations.
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating undrained Young's modulus for fine-grained (clay) soils in design.

sections.title: Typical Values
sections.summary: Provides typical ranges of undrained Young's modulus (Eu) normalized by atmospheric pressure (Pa) for clays of varying consistency — from very soft to clay shale — based on USACE (1990) and Kulhawy and Mayne (1990). Values span 5 to 2000 Pa depending on consistency and source.
sections.body: Typical values of undrained Young's modulus are summarized in Table 8-19.
key_points: Eu/Pa ranges from 5–50 for very soft clay to 1000–2000 for clay shale (USACE 1990).
Kulhawy and Mayne (1990) provide narrower ranges: 15–40 (soft) to 80–200 (stiff/silty).
Sandy clays have a wide USACE range of 250–2000; no Kulhawy and Mayne value is given.
Values are normalized by atmospheric pressure (Pa) for dimensional consistency.
sections.applicability: Applies when a preliminary estimate of undrained Young's modulus is needed for clays based on consistency alone.

sections.title: Correlations with Undrained Shear Strength
sections.summary: Presents the Duncan and Buchignani (1987) correlation for the ratio of undrained Young's modulus to undrained shear strength (Eu/su) as a function of plasticity index (PI) and overconsolidation ratio (OCR), based on direct simple shear test results. Shown graphically in Figure 8-51.
sections.body: Duncan and Buchignani (1987) proposed a correlation to obtain the ratio of the undrained shear modulus to the undrained shear strength for fine grained soils as a function of the plasticity index and overconsolidation ratio as shown in Figure 8-51. This correlation is based on results obtained from direct simple shear tests.
key_points: Eu/su ratio is a function of plasticity index (PI) and overconsolidation ratio (OCR) per Duncan and Buchignani (1987).
Correlation is based on direct simple shear test results.
Figure 8-51 provides the graphical relationship for design use.
Higher OCR and lower PI generally yield higher Eu/su ratios.
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating undrained Young's modulus for fine-grained soils using known undrained shear strength, PI, and OCR.

sections.title: Correlations with Standard Penetration and Pressuremeter Tests
sections.summary: Describes the use of pressuremeter test (PMT) to directly measure horizontal soil modulus in clays, which is approximately equal to undrained Young's modulus. Presents the Ohya et al. (1982) correlation between PMT modulus (EPMT) and SPT N value in Figure 8-52, noting significant scatter (r² = 0.39).
sections.body:
The pressuremeter test is used to directly measure a soil modulus in the horizontal direction. According to Kulhawy and Mayne (1990), the horizontal modulus measured in clay using the pressuremeter test is approximately equal to the undrained Young's modulus.

Ohya et al. (1982) presented the relationship for the undrained Young's modulus from the pressuremeter (EPMT) and the SPT N value shown in Figure 8-52. The relationship shown in this figure exhibits a large amount of scatter (r² = 0.39), and it should be used with caution.
key_points: PMT directly measures horizontal soil modulus; in clays this is approximately equal to undrained Young's modulus (Kulhawy and Mayne 1990).
Ohya et al. (1982) correlation relates EPMT to SPT N value for clays (Figure 8-52).
Correlation has high scatter (r² = 0.39) and should be used with caution.
SPT-based estimates of Eu for clays are inherently uncertain due to scatter.
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating undrained Young's modulus of clays from pressuremeter or SPT N values.

sections.title: Correlations to Load Tests
sections.summary: Presents two sets of correlations for undrained Young's modulus of clays back-calculated from load tests: Poulos and Davis (1980) for drilled shafts and driven piles as a function of undrained shear strength (Figure 8-53), and Callanan and Kulhawy (1985) for drilled shafts and spread foundations (Figure 8-54) with normalization by mean vertical stress.
sections.body:
Poulos and Davis (1980) presented the relationship for the undrained Young's modulus calculated from load tests on drilled shafts and driven piles as a function of the undrained shear strength of the clay, as shown in Figure 8-53.

Callanan and Kulhawy (1985) presented the relationship for the undrained Young's modulus of clays back calculated from load tests on drilled shafts and spread foundations presented in Figure 8-54. In the right side of Figure 8-54, σvm is the mean total vertical stress over the foundation depth.
key_points: Poulos and Davis (1980) relate Eu to undrained shear strength for drilled shafts and driven piles in compression (Figure 8-53).
Callanan and Kulhawy (1985) provide Eu correlations for drilled shafts (compression and uplift) and spread foundations (uplift) (Figure 8-54).
For spread foundations, Eu is normalized by the mean total vertical stress (σvm) over foundation depth.
Load test back-calculations offer site-specific modulus estimates that may be more reliable than index correlations.
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating undrained Young's modulus for clays supporting deep foundations or spread foundations using load test data.

sections.title: Drained Young's Modulus of Coarse-Grained Soils
sections.summary: Covers estimation of drained Young's modulus (E) for coarse-grained soils, which experience undrained conditions only briefly. Provides typical ranges of E normalized by atmospheric pressure by relative density (loose, medium, dense) and soil type from Poulos (1975) and USACE (1990), and introduces SPT-based correlations in the subsection below.
sections.body: Coarse-grained soils only experience undrained conditions for a very short period of time and under special circumstances. For this reason, the Young's modulus is only required for drained conditions in most cases. Typical values of drained Young's modulus (E) based on relative density are summarized in Table 8-20 for coarse-grained soils.
key_points: Coarse-grained soils are analyzed using drained Young's modulus in virtually all practical cases.
E/Pa ranges from 100–200 (loose) to 500–1000 (dense) per Poulos (1975); USACE (1990) gives higher values for driven pile conditions.
Silty sand has a wide typical range of 250–2000 Pa (USACE 1990).
Values are normalized by atmospheric pressure (Pa) for non-dimensionalization.
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating drained Young's modulus for coarse-grained soils (sands, gravels, silty sands) based on relative density.

sections.title: Correlations with SPT N Values
sections.summary: Presents multiple published correlations for estimating drained Young's modulus of coarse-grained soils from SPT N values, compiled in Table 8-21 and plotted in Figure 8-55. Correlations from Ferrent (1963), Webb (1969), Begemann (1974), and Kulhawy and Mayne (1990) cover sands, clayey sands, silts with sand, and gravels with sand under NC and OC conditions.
sections.body:
Many different correlations have been developed to estimate the drained Young's modulus of coarse-grained soils using SPT N values. Some of these correlations are presented in Table 8-21 and plotted in Figure 8-55.

E = drained Young's modulus,
Pa = atmospheric pressure (in same units as E),
N = SPT blow count value (use N60 for modern samplers),
ν = Poisson's ratio, and
C = empirical coefficient equal to 3 for silts with sand and 12 for gravel with sand.
key_points: Multiple correlations exist for drained E of coarse-grained soils from SPT N; all normalize E by atmospheric pressure (Pa).
Ferrent (1963): E ≈ 7.1(1−ν²)·N·Pa for sandy soils.
Webb (1969): E ≈ 4.7(N+15)·Pa for sands; E ≈ 3.1(N+5)·Pa for clayey sands.
Begemann (1974): E ≈ C(N+6)·Pa for N<15; E ≈ C(N+6)−39.5·Pa for N≥15, with C depending on soil type.
Kulhawy and Mayne (1990): E ≈ 5·N60·Pa (sands with fines), 10·N60·Pa (NC clean sands), 15·N60·Pa (OC clean sands).
N60 (energy-corrected blow count) should be used for modern samplers per Kulhawy and Mayne (1990).
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating drained Young's modulus for coarse-grained soils (sands, silts with sand, gravels with sand) using SPT N values.

sections.title: CALIFORNIA BEARING RATIO (CBR)
sections.summary: Introduces the California Bearing Ratio (CBR) as a penetration test (ASTM D1883) developed by the California DOT to assess load-bearing capacity of soils for road construction. Notes that CBR is primarily a lab test but can also be measured in the field, and that specimens may be soaked or tested at compaction water content. Cautions that correlations apply to specific soil types and original references should be consulted.
sections.body: The California bearing ratio (CBR) is a penetration test developed by the California Department of Transportation to assess the load-bearing capacity of soils used for building roads. This test is described in ASTM D1883. The CBR is predominately a laboratory test, but there are methods available to measure CBR in the field. CBR can be determined for test specimens that have been soaked, or specimens at their compaction water content. Because these correlations apply to specific soil types, the original references should be consulted before using the correlations.
key_points: CBR is a penetration test standardized in ASTM D1883, originally developed by the California Department of Transportation.
CBR is primarily a lab test but field methods also exist.
Test specimens may be evaluated soaked or at their compaction water content.
All empirical correlations in this section are soil-type specific; original references must be consulted before application.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever CBR is being determined or estimated for soils used in road or pavement subgrade design.

sections.title: Correlations with Index and Compaction Properties
sections.summary: Presents empirical correlations for estimating CBR from index properties (grain size, Atterberg limits, unit weight, specific gravity, angle of repose) in Table 8-22, and from compaction properties (dry unit weight ratio and water content ratio relative to Modified Proctor values) in Table 8-23. Covers both soaked and unsoaked conditions across multiple researchers.
sections.body: Several researchers have presented correlations to estimate the CBR using index properties. Correlations to grain size, Atterberg limits, and other index properties are summarized in Table 8-22. Correlations between CBR and soil compaction properties are summarized in Table 8-23.
key_points: CBR can be estimated from fines content and plasticity index: CBR = 75 / (1 + 0.728 × FC×PI) when FC×PI = 0 per NCHRP (2001).
Gravel content, liquid limit, plastic limit, dry/moist unit weight, specific gravity, and angle of repose are all used in various CBR correlations (Table 8-22).
Compaction-based correlations (Table 8-23) use the ratio of dry unit weight to maximum dry unit weight and water content to optimum water content from the Modified Proctor test.
Water contents in compaction correlations must be expressed consistently — both decimal or both percentage form.
Correlations cover both soaked and unsoaked CBR conditions.
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating CBR from readily available index properties or compaction test results (Modified Proctor) without performing a direct CBR test.

sections.title: Correlations with Dynamic Cone Penetration
sections.summary: Provides empirical power-law and alternative correlations between CBR and the Dynamic Cone Penetration (DCP) index. The general form CBR = A·DCP^x is tabulated for numerous researchers (Table 8-24) with varying A and x coefficients. A separate nonlinear correlation by Nazzal (2003) is given for DCP values between 6.3 and 67 mm/blow. Figure 8-56 shows the expected range of CBR predictions.
sections.body:
Many correlations have been developed to estimate CBR from the results of dynamic cone penetration tests. Most of these correlations can take the form

CBR = A · DCP^x  (8-37)

where:
CBR = California Bearing Ratio,
A = empirical coefficient,
DCP = dynamic cone penetration index (mm/blow), and
x = empirical exponent.

The values of A and x found by various researchers are summarized in Table 8-24. The range of CBR values expected from these correlations is presented in Figure 8-56.

Nazzal (2003) developed a similar correlation to those in Table 8-24 for soils with DCP values between 6.3 and 67 mm/blow:

CBR = 2559 / (1 + 7.35 · DCP^1.84) - 1  (8-38)

where:
CBR = California Bearing Ratio, and
DCP = dynamic cone penetration index (mm/blow).
key_points: The general DCP-CBR relationship is a power law: CBR = A·DCP^x, where A and x are empirically determined coefficients (Eq. 8-37).
Coefficients A and x vary widely by researcher and soil type; A ranges from 25 to 501 and x ranges from -0.55 to -2.00 (Table 8-24).
Nazzal (2003) provides a nonlinear alternative (Eq. 8-38) valid for DCP values of 6.3–67 mm/blow.
Figure 8-56 illustrates the scatter in predicted CBR across multiple DCP correlations, highlighting uncertainty in selection.
Some correlations are soil-type specific (e.g., fine-grained, coarse-grained, CL with CBR < 10).

equations.description: General power-law correlation between CBR and DCP index: CBR = A · DCP^x, where A is an empirical coefficient and x is an empirical exponent.
Nazzal (2003) nonlinear CBR–DCP correlation for DCP values between 6.3 and 67 mm/blow: CBR = 2559 / (1 + 7.35·DCP^1.84) − 1.

sections.applicability: Applies when estimating CBR from Dynamic Cone Penetration (DCP) test results in the field or laboratory, particularly for pavement subgrade evaluation.

sections.title: Correlations with Standard Penetration Test
sections.summary: Presents a logarithmic correlation by Livneh (1989) for estimating CBR from SPT blow count (N), with supporting data in Figure 8-57. The equation relates log(CBR) to log(N60), and is applicable using N60 for modern hammers. Provides a direct link between the most commonly performed in-situ test and pavement subgrade capacity.
sections.body:
Livneh (1989) found that the CBR could be estimated from the results of the Standard Penetration Test as shown below. The data used to obtain this correlation is presented in Figure 8-57.

log(CBR) = −0.26 + log[(300 · N − 5.13) / 6.55]  (8-39)

where:
CBR = California Bearing Ratio, and
N = SPT blow count value (use N60 for modern hammers).
key_points: Livneh (1989) developed a log-log correlation between CBR and SPT blow count N (Eq. 8-39).
N60 should be used for modern hammer systems to standardize energy input.
Figure 8-57 presents the original data supporting this correlation.
This correlation enables CBR estimation directly from routine SPT data without additional testing.

equations.description: Livneh (1989) logarithmic correlation between CBR and SPT blow count: log(CBR) = −0.26 + log[(300·N − 5.13) / 6.55], where N = SPT blow count (N60 for modern hammers).

sections.applicability: Applies when estimating CBR from Standard Penetration Test (SPT) results, particularly where direct CBR measurements are unavailable but SPT data exists.

sections.title: Hydraulic Conductivity
sections.summary: Introduces hydraulic conductivity (coefficient of permeability) as the parameter governing flow rate and head loss through a soil mass. Highlights the extremely wide range of values across soil types (Table 8-25) and explains why variable ground conditions make accurate evaluation difficult. Points the reader to subsections on typical values and correlations for coarse- and fine-grained soils.
sections.body: The hydraulic conductivity (a.k.a., the coefficient of permeability) governs the flow rate and head loss as water flows through a soil mass. The hydraulic conductivity has one of the widest ranges of any engineering parameter as can be seen in Table 8-25. The wide range of possible values and the influence of variable ground conditions on the hydraulic conductivity make this parameter difficult to evaluate with a high degree of accuracy.
key_points: Hydraulic conductivity governs flow rate and head loss through a soil mass.
Values span many orders of magnitude — one of the widest ranges of any engineering parameter.
Variable ground conditions make high-accuracy evaluation difficult.
Typical values by soil type are tabulated in Table 8-25.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever hydraulic conductivity must be characterized for any soil type in geotechnical analysis.

sections.title: Typical Values
sections.summary: Provides typical ranges of hydraulic conductivity classified by soil type, from gravel (>10⁻³ m/s, high permeability) through clay (<10⁻⁹ m/s, practically impermeable), as tabulated in Table 8-25 (after Terzaghi et al. 1996). Directs the reader to Section 6-3.3 for additional typical values.
sections.body: Typical values of hydraulic conductivity based on soil type are presented in Table 8-25. Other typical values based on soil type can be found in Section 6-3.3.
key_points: Gravel: k > 10⁻³ m/s (high permeability).
Sandy gravel: k = 10⁻³ to 10⁻⁵ m/s (medium permeability).
Clean to fine sands: k = 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁷ m/s (low permeability).
Silt and silty clay: k = 10⁻⁷ to 10⁻⁹ m/s (very low permeability).
Clay: k < 10⁻⁹ m/s (practically impermeable).
Additional typical values by soil type are in Section 6-3.3.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting or checking preliminary hydraulic conductivity values by USCS soil classification.

sections.title: Correlations for Coarse-Grained Soils
sections.summary: Presents multiple empirical correlations for estimating hydraulic conductivity of coarse-grained soils from grain-size parameters. Covers the Hazen (1911) D10-based formula for clean sands (Eq. 8-40), the USACE (1993) horizontal permeability chart for Mississippi Valley SP/SW sands (Figure 8-58), Kenney et al. (1984) D5-based correlation (Figure 8-59), a combined D5/D10/Cu/e chart (Figure 8-60), and the modified Kozeny-Carman equation by Carrier (2003) using the full grain-size distribution (Eq. 8-41).
sections.body:
One of the first correlations to estimate the hydraulic conductivity based on grain size was presented by Hazen (1911). This correlation was developed for saturated clean sands with a fines content less than 5% and D10 values ranging from 0.1 mm to 3 mm:

k = C · (D10)²  (Eq. 8-40)

Where: k = hydraulic conductivity (cm/s), C = empirical coefficient, usually taken to be 1 cm/s/mm², and D10 = grain size corresponding to 10% passing on the grain-size distribution (mm).

Based on data from the middle and lower Mississippi River Valley, the USACE (1993) correlated the in situ horizontal permeability of fine to medium, relatively uniform sands (USCS classifications of SP or SW) as shown in Figure 8-58. This correlation was recommended for use only within the geographic area for which it was developed.

Kenney et al. (1984) correlated the hydraulic conductivity of coarse-grained soils to the grain size corresponding to 5% passing on the cumulative grain-size distribution curve (D5), as shown in Figure 8-59. A similar correlation can be developed between the hydraulic conductivity for clean coarse-grained soils and the D10 grain size as shown in Figure 8-60.

Carrier (2003) presented a modified version of the Kozeny-Carman equation (Kozeny 1927; Carman 1938, 1956) to estimate the hydraulic conductivity using the full grain-size distribution of a soil. The modifications introduced by Carrier (2003) to the original equation simplify its use. The hydraulic conductivity can be estimated by Eq. 8-41:

k = 1.99×10⁻² · [e³/(1+e)] · [100% / Σ(fi / (Dli^0.404 · Dsi^0.596))]² · (1 / S²)  (cm/s)

where: k = hydraulic conductivity (cm/s), fi = fraction of particles (by mass) between two adjacent sieve sizes, Dli = the particle size of the coarser sieve (mm), Dsi = the particle size of the finer sieve (mm), S = surface area factor ranging from 6 for spheres to 8.5 for angular particles, and e = void ratio.

Additional discussion and correlations of k to grain size can be found in Section 6-3.3.
key_points: Hazen (1911) formula (Eq. 8-40): k = C·D10²; valid for clean sands with <5% fines and D10 between 0.1–3 mm.
USACE (1993) correlation (Figure 8-58) applies specifically to SP/SW sands from the middle and lower Mississippi River Valley.
Kenney et al. (1984) correlate k to D5 (Figure 8-59); a D10-based analog is provided in Figure 8-60.
Carrier (2003) modified Kozeny-Carman equation (Eq. 8-41) uses the full grain-size distribution, void ratio, and particle shape factor.
Surface area factor S ranges from 6 (spherical particles) to 8.5 (angular particles) in the Carrier equation.
USACE (1993) chart is geographically restricted to the Mississippi River Valley region.

equations.description: Hazen (1911) correlation: k = C·(D10)², estimating hydraulic conductivity (cm/s) of clean sands from D10 grain size (mm); C ≈ 1 cm/s/mm².
Carrier (2003) modified Kozeny-Carman equation estimating hydraulic conductivity (cm/s) from the full grain-size distribution, void ratio, and particle shape factor S.

sections.applicability: Applies when estimating hydraulic conductivity of coarse-grained soils (sands, gravels) from grain-size distribution data and/or void ratio.

sections.title: Correlations for Fine-Grained Soils
sections.summary: Presents empirical correlations for estimating hydraulic conductivity of fine-grained soils using Atterberg limits, void ratio, and compaction properties. Covers the Carrier and Beckman (1984) equation relating k to PL, PI, and void ratio (Eq. 8-42); the Benson et al. (1994) equation for compacted clay liners using PI, gravel content, clay fraction, compactor weight, and compaction state (Eq. 8-43); and the Benson and Trast (1995) equation for compacted clays using PI, clay fraction, and compactive effort index (Eq. 8-44). Cautions that these correlations should be used carefully.
sections.body:
Unlike coarse-grained soils, the hydraulic conductivity of fine-grained soils is difficult to estimate from index properties. Hydraulic conductivity correlations for fine-grained soils should be used with caution.

Carrier and Beckman (1984) related the hydraulic conductivity and the Atterberg limits and void ratio of fine-grained soils using Eq. 8-42:

k = [(e - 0.027·PL - 0.242·PI) / (PI · (1 + e))]^4.29 · 0.0174  (m/s)

where: k = hydraulic conductivity (m/s), e = void ratio, PL = plastic limit, and PI = plasticity index.

Benson et al. (1994) measured the hydraulic conductivity on intact test specimens obtained from compacted clay liners from 67 landfills in North America. The results of those tests were found to relate to other measured properties of the clays using Eq. 8-43:

ln(k) = -18.35 + 0.08·PI - 2.87·GC - 0.32·CF + W + 894·[γd / (Gs·γw) / (1 - γd/(Gs·γw))]

where: k = hydraulic conductivity (m/s), CF = clay-sized fraction (percent by mass smaller than 0.002 mm), GC = gravel content = percent retained between 75 mm and #4 sieve, W = weight of field compactor (kN), PI = plasticity index, w = molding water content, γw = unit weight of water, γd = dry unit weight, and Gs = specific gravity of solids.

Benson and Trast (1995) performed hydraulic conductivity tests on 13 compacted clays used for compacted clay liners around the United States. The test specimens were prepared at different water contents, compacted, and then tested to measure the hydraulic conductivity. The results were correlated by Benson and Trast to k using Eq. 8-44:

ln(k) = -15 - 0.087·PI - 0.054·CF + 0.022·E - 0.91 + [γd / (Gs·γw) / (1 - γd/(Gs·γw))]

where: k = hydraulic conductivity (m/s), w = molding water content, γw = unit weight of water, γd = dry unit weight, Gs = specific gravity of solids, PI = plasticity index, CF = clay-sized fraction, and E = compactive effort index (equal to -1, 0, and 1 for modified, standard, and reduced Proctor compactive effort, respectively).
key_points: Hydraulic conductivity of fine-grained soils cannot be reliably estimated from index properties alone — all correlations should be used with caution.
Carrier and Beckman (1984) (Eq. 8-42) uses plastic limit, plasticity index, and void ratio to estimate k in m/s.
Benson et al. (1994) (Eq. 8-43) was developed from 67 North American landfill compacted clay liner specimens; incorporates PI, gravel content, clay fraction, compactor weight, and compaction state.
Benson and Trast (1995) (Eq. 8-44) uses PI, clay-sized fraction, and a compactive effort index (E = -1 modified, 0 standard, +1 reduced Proctor).
All three fine-grained correlations output k in m/s and require void ratio or dry unit weight information.

equations.description: Carrier and Beckman (1984) correlation: estimates hydraulic conductivity (m/s) of fine-grained soils from plastic limit (PL), plasticity index (PI), and void ratio (e).

Benson et al. (1994) correlation: estimates ln(k) in m/s for compacted clay liners using PI, gravel content (GC), clay-sized fraction (CF), compactor weight (W), molding water content, dry unit weight, and specific gravity.

Benson and Trast (1995) correlation: estimates ln(k) in m/s for compacted clays using PI, clay-sized fraction (CF), compactive effort index (E), molding water content, dry unit weight, and specific gravity.

sections.applicability: Applies when estimating hydraulic conductivity of fine-grained soils (clays, silts) particularly compacted clay liner materials, using Atterberg limits, void ratio, and compaction parameters.

sections.title: Shear Wave Velocity
sections.summary: Parent section covering methods for estimating shear wave velocity (Vs) from in-situ tests. Contains two subsections addressing SPT-based and CPT-based correlations, respectively. Provides the general framework for Vs estimation used in geotechnical and seismic site response analyses.
key_points: Shear wave velocity (Vs) can be estimated from in-situ test data using empirical correlations.
Two primary in-situ test types are addressed: Standard Penetration Test (SPT) and Cone Penetration Test (CPT).
Both SPT and CPT correlations are compiled from multiple literature sources and summarized in tables.
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating shear wave velocity (Vs) from SPT or CPT data for geotechnical or seismic site characterization.

sections.title: Correlations with Standard Penetration Test
sections.summary: Presents empirical correlations for estimating shear wave velocity (Vs) from SPT N values. The general power-law form (Eq. 8-45) uses empirical coefficients B, x, and y along with blow count N and depth z. Numerous literature-sourced coefficient sets are tabulated in Table 8-26 (N and depth) and Table 8-27 (N only), with Figure 8-61 showing the range of predicted Vs values.
sections.body:
Many correlations have been developed to estimate the shear wave velocity (Vs) from SPT N values. Judgment is required regarding the use of uncorrected vs. corrected blow count. Older correlations were likely developed using 60% hammer efficiency as represented by N60. The general form for most of the Vs correlations is:

Vs = B * N^x * z^y  (Eq. 8-45)

where:
Vs = shear wave velocity (m/s),
B, x, and y = empirical coefficients,
N = SPT blow count, and
z = depth to the soil layer (m).

Correlations using the form of Equation 8-45 are summarized in Table 8-26. Other correlations are presented in Table 8-27. The range of values expected from these correlations can be seen in Figure 8-61.
key_points: The general SPT-Vs correlation form is Vs = B·N^x·z^y (Eq. 8-45), with empirical coefficients B, x, and y varying by soil type and reference.
Judgment is required regarding use of uncorrected N vs. corrected N60; older correlations were likely based on N60 (60% hammer efficiency).
Table 8-26 compiles over 30 sets of B, x, y coefficients from the literature, covering sands, clays, silts, and gravels.
Table 8-27 provides additional correlations in non-standard forms, including normalized Vs,1 and N1,60cs-based equations.
Figure 8-61 shows the full range of predicted Vs values across the compiled correlations, illustrating prediction uncertainty.

equations.description: General power-law form for estimating shear wave velocity from SPT blow count and depth: Vs = B·N^x·z^y, where Vs is in m/s, N is SPT blow count, z is depth in m, and B, x, y are empirical coefficients.

sections.title: Correlations with Cone Penetration Test
sections.summary: Summarizes empirical correlations for estimating shear wave velocity (Vs) directly from CPT results, including cone tip resistance (qc), sleeve friction (fs), void ratio (e), depth (z), effective vertical stress (σ′v), and soil behavior index (Ic). Table 8-28 compiles over a dozen equations from multiple references covering sands, clays, and general soils. Notes that some CPT cones can measure Vs directly via geophone or accelerometer.
sections.body: Several correlations relating the shear wave velocity to the results of the cone penetration test have been developed and are summarized in Table 8-28. It should be noted that some cones are equipped with a geophone or accelerometer and can measure shear wave velocity directly.
key_points: Multiple CPT-Vs correlations exist using qc, fs, void ratio, depth, effective stress, and soil behavior index Ic as inputs.
Table 8-28 consolidates equations from over ten references, differentiating by soil type (sands, clays, general).
Normalized parameters include Vs,1 = Vs·(Pa/σ′v)^0.25 and qc1 = (qc/Pa)·(Pa/σ′v)^n, where n depends on Ic.
Some CPT cones equipped with geophones or accelerometers can directly measure Vs, bypassing correlation uncertainty.
The exponent n in qc1 normalization is 0.5 for Ic < 2.6 and 0.75 otherwise, per Robertson (2009) and Ulmer et al. (2020).

key_points: Covers all symbols used in Chapter 8, from basic soil indices (LL, PI, CF) to in-situ test parameters (qc, N60, KD, Vs).
Includes consolidation and compressibility parameters (Cc, Cr, Cα, cv, Mds) with their modified and intrinsic variants.
Defines bearing capacity factors (Nc, Nk, Nkt, Nq) and CPT-specific symbols (qc,NC, qc,OC, R) for sand and clay interpretations.
Stress notation distinguishes total stress (σv), effective stress (σʹv), and preconsolidation pressure (σʹp).
Several symbols carry dual meanings (e.g., E = Young's modulus and compactive effort index; a = CPT net area ratio and power-function coefficient).
Equation-specific coefficients (A, f, α, x, y, W) are explicitly referenced to their source equations (8-37, 8-33, 8-34, 8-45, 8-43).
